q: Calculate the percentage change for 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 mol dm⁻³.
Explain why percentage change is used instead of change in mass.
The cylinders started with different masses, so percentages allow a fair comparison.
Estimate the sucrose concentration with the same water potential as the potato cells. Show how.
Zero change lies between 0.2 (+5.0) and 0.4 (-1.9): 0.2 + 0.2 × 5.0 / 6.9 = about 0.35 mol dm⁻³ (or read off a graph).
Explain the results at 0.0 and at 0.6 mol dm⁻³.
At 0.0 the solution has a higher water potential than the cells, so water enters by osmosis and the cells become turgid. At 0.6 it is lower, so water leaves and the cells begin to plasmolyse.
The losses at 0.8 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³ are almost the same. Suggest why.
The cells have already lost almost all the water that can leave: they are fully plasmolysed, so a stronger solution cannot remove much more.

21.t: Working with data: red blood cells in salt
q: Estimate the salt concentration at which half the untreated cells burst.
Explain why red blood cells burst in low salt concentrations.
The solution has a higher water potential than the cells, so water enters by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall, so the membrane bursts.
Compare the two curves and explain the effect of blocking aquaporins.
Fewer cells burst at every concentration (at 0.3%: 30% against 85%). Without aquaporins water enters more slowly, so fewer cells have burst after 10 minutes.
Explain why 0.9% salt is used in hospital drips.
It has the same water potential as blood plasma (isotonic), so there is no net water movement and cells keep their shape.
Predict what red blood cells look like in 3% salt. Explain.
They shrink and look wrinkled or spiky (crenated), because water leaves by osmosis.
